steps.intro: The promo film redrew the buddy's faces in a warmer style, and you said those would be the guideline for every theme in the app. None of it has reached the app yet — it lives only in the film's own tooling and, drawn a second time by hand, on the website. Before anything gets drawn, five decisions. Every one of them changes what you'll see on screen. There are five characters in play, not seven or eleven — most themes share one.

steps.path: The buddy in the corner, and every theme's own character
steps.headline: How far should the mascot redraw go — every character, or only the two the film already redrew?
steps.today: The buddy's face comes from a small set of drawings. Seven of your themes have no character of their own and all share ONE built-in default character: Light, Dark, Midnight, Creme, Cotton Candy Sky, Meadow Mist and Devil's Garden. Four community themes draw their own: Golden Sunbreak, Halftone Dimension, Kuromi Dreamer and Strawberry Kitty.
steps.problem: Those faces were drawn early and never revisited. The 'shocked' face is two big black discs and a black hole for a mouth, and the resting face has its eyes squeezed shut. Your words during the promo were that the eyes looked scary. The film only redrew two of the five characters: the default one, and Golden Sunbreak (which happens to share the default's face shape, so it came along for free).
steps.proposal: Redraw faces in the film's warmer style — expression carried by eyebrows, eyelids and mouth instead of by the size of a black circle. The question is how far that goes. Halftone keeps its glowing visor and the two cats keep their cat faces either way; you already said those ARE their characters.

options.label: All five characters, each in its own style
pros: No theme is left behind — switching themes never makes the app look older
The cats stay cats and Halftone keeps its visor; they just stop looking frightened
The default character covers seven themes at once, so most users see it immediately
cons: Three characters have to be redrawn by hand rather than adapted, so more rounds of you looking at drawings
Halftone's visor and the cats' faces have no eyebrows to work with, so the new style has to be reinterpreted for each

options.label: Only the default character and Golden Sunbreak
pros: Fastest by a long way — both are already drawn, it is a port rather than new art
Still reaches eight of the eleven themes, including every built-in one
cons: Kuromi, Strawberry Kitty and Halftone keep the scary faces, so installing one of them visibly downgrades the app
Those are the three most distinctive characters you have — the ones people install a theme FOR

options.label: All five, plus brand-new characters for the three themes that have none
pros: Cotton Candy Sky, Meadow Mist and Devil's Garden stop borrowing a character that does not match them
Every theme becomes a complete little world rather than a colour scheme
cons: By far the biggest job — three characters invented from nothing, not just re-faced
Those three are community themes; inventing characters for them is a decision about someone else's theme

steps.path: The buddy's face in the corner of the chat window
steps.headline: Should the buddy get three new faces — happy, smug and shut-down — that a theme can draw?
steps.today: Every character has exactly six faces: resting, welcome, curious, shocked, dizzy, and blink. That list is fixed by the app — a theme cannot add to it.
steps.problem: The film added three more faces — happy, smug, and shut-down (eyes closed, arms and legs tucked in). They only exist inside the film's own tooling. The app has no slot for them, so even if a theme drew them the app could never show them. The film's buddy is a richer character than the one in your app.
steps.proposal: Add the three new faces to the list a theme can supply. A theme that doesn't draw them falls back to one it does have, so nothing breaks for existing themes or for anyone's installed theme.

options.label: Add all three
pros: He can look pleased when work finishes, instead of only neutral or startled
'Shut down' gives him a visible way to go quiet, which the sleep question below needs
Old themes keep working untouched — they just fall back to a face they already have
cons: Every character now has nine faces to draw instead of six, on top of redrawing the six
Theme makers have more to do before their theme feels complete

options.label: Add only 'happy'
pros: The one face the app has an obvious daily use for — work finished, all good
Half the extra drawing
cons: No way to show him powering down, so sleeping has to reuse 'blink', which just looks like he blinked and got stuck

options.label: Keep the six he has
pros: Nothing new to draw for any theme
cons: He can never look pleased about anything
The film's character stays better than the app's, permanently

steps.path: The buddy's face in the corner of the chat window
steps.headline: Should his resting face have open, awake eyes instead of the closed squint?
steps.today: When nothing is happening, the buddy's resting face is a closed-eye squint — two curved lines like >< . It is the very first face anyone sees.
steps.problem: His eyes are shut when he is doing nothing, which reads as asleep or not paying attention. The film's warm set has no squint at all; its resting face is open eyes with a highlight, the one labelled 'welcome'.
steps.proposal: Make his resting face the open, awake one, and keep the squint for a moment — a happy scrunch when something goes well, rather than his default state.

options.label: Open, awake eyes at rest
pros: He looks present and ready rather than asleep
Matches the film and the website, so the app stops being the odd one out
The eyes have highlights, which is most of what makes the new style read as warm
cons: A character always looking at you is more presence in the corner of the screen; some people find that more distracting than a closed-eyed one

options.label: Keep the closed squint at rest
pros: Calmest possible resting state
Nothing to change
cons: The first impression of the app is a character with its eyes shut
Everywhere else he appears — the permission screen, the moved screen, Settings, the mini-game — he is asleep too

steps.path: The buddy in the corner of the chat window
steps.headline: Should the buddy show what the app is doing, or only idle more richly?
steps.today: When you are not touching him, the buddy breathes, blinks and sways a little. His face changes only when you drag him, or when something needs your attention.
steps.problem: He does not respond to what the app is actually doing. He looks exactly the same while it is thinking, when it finishes your work, and when something has failed. All the character is in how he moves when you grab him.
steps.proposal: Give him reactions to the app's own activity. The film already contains a library of movements built for this — waving, cheering, shrugging, nodding, thinking, being startled — that has never been ported into the app. How far it goes is the question. Whichever you pick, the existing 'reduce motion' setting still turns all of it off.

options.label: Idling, plus reactions to what the app is doing
pros: You can tell at a glance whether it is working, done, or stuck — without reading any text
Most useful when the buddy is small in a corner and the words are too tiny to scan
Uses movements that already exist and were already tuned for the film
cons: Movement at the edge of your vision while you are trying to concentrate
If a reaction is wrong or late it is worse than no reaction — a cheering buddy over a failed run

options.label: Richer idling only — no reactions
pros: Never distracting and never wrong, because it never claims anything
Cheapest, and cannot mislead you about what the app is doing
cons: He stays a decoration; you still have to look at the text to know anything
'Slightly more alive' would mean only a wider variety of blinking

options.label: Reactions, plus spontaneous moments of his own
pros: The most character — he yawns, stretches, notices your cursor
Feels like a companion rather than a status light
cons: Movement with no meaning trains you to ignore him, which then hides the reactions that DO mean something
Highest chance of crossing from charming to annoying, and the line is different for every person

steps.path: The buddy in the corner of the chat window
steps.headline: Should the buddy curl up and sleep after a stretch of quiet?
steps.today: The buddy breathes and sways forever. He never stops, however long you leave the app alone.
steps.problem: A character that never rests reads as a screensaver rather than a companion — and on a laptop something animating forever in a corner is drawing power for nothing.
steps.proposal: After a stretch of quiet he curls up and sleeps, using the new 'shut down' face — eyes closed, arms and legs tucked in. Anything happening wakes him.

options.label: Sleeps after a few quiet minutes, wakes on any activity
pros: Reads as a real little creature: he rests when there is nothing to do
Stops the animation entirely while you are away, so no battery drain for a character nobody is watching
Waking up IS a reaction — you notice something started
cons: If the wake-up is slow or missed he looks broken rather than asleep
Depends on the 'shut down' face existing, so this is tied to the question above

options.label: Sleeps only when the app window is not the one you are using
pros: He is always awake whenever you are actually looking at the app
Saves the same power, since that is when you are away
cons: You would rarely see him sleep, so most of the charm of it is lost
Switching windows constantly would have him nodding off and waking repeatedly

options.label: Never sleeps
pros: He is always there and always the same
cons: Animation runs forever for no one
No resting state, so 'shut down' has no everyday use
